cases.input: the deploy is blocked on the migration
cases.note: A non-empty message is a push, and the whole reply is the acknowledgement. Anchored at both ends on purpose: the failure this catches is not a wrong word, it is a model that answers correctly and then adds 'I've added that to the stack. Anything else?'. That extra sentence is what makes a deterministic-looking bot read as a chatbot wearing its name.

An empty message pops. The grader cannot name the entry -- the stack is agent-global and durable, so what comes back depends on what this agent was told earlier, which is the point of the bundle and not something a case may pin. It asserts the SHAPE: the marker, then a non-empty payload. An empty stack answers 'Squawk stack is empty.' and fails this pattern, which is correct: a case that accepted both would assert nothing.

Trimming decides push versus pop, so whitespace must take the pop branch. Either pop outcome passes here because the stack's contents are not fixed; what is being asserted is that three spaces did NOT get pushed as an entry. The failure mode is a bundle that tests `if message:` instead of `if message.strip():` and quietly accumulates blank rows.

The case a text matcher cannot carry. `Squawk!` with nothing after it is a well-formed PUSH acknowledgement and a meaningless pop, and no pattern can tell the two apart once the payload is optional -- so grading the answer text cannot catch a model that skips the store and answers from the conversation it can already see. This grades the trajectory instead: an empty message must have read `squawk/stack`. It is deterministic, which the graders here are required to be (an LLM judge is deferred to ADR-0042 precisely so eval results stay reproducible). RESIDUAL LIMIT: trajectory records the tool REQUEST, so this proves the pop consulted the stack, not that the entry it returned is the one that was stored.
